title: So what does work?
author: Mark Enser
summary: In the closing instalment of his Supporting Unwilling Writers series, Mark Enser takes on the question every training session ends with: what actually works? His honest answer is that the research does not hand over a single practice, because across the series promising approaches kept shrinking at scale, contradicting one another, or resting on thin evidence. He widens the lens with Lortie-Forgues and Inglis, whose review of 141 large trials found an average effect of 0.06 standard deviations and about 40% of trials uninformative. His move is to shift from practices to principles, since a practice is what you do and a principle is the reason it works when it does. He offers six principles for unwilling writers, each stating what it rules out, from finding the barrier before choosing the fix to judging pupils by what they can do without help. He closes with six questions to put to any writing claim and revisits the series title, concluding that unwilling described what was seen rather than why.
points: Writing interventions repeatedly shrank at scale, contradicted each other or relied on thin evidence, so no single practice can be promised to work.
Education trials in general show small and often uninformative effects, and writing adds problems of mixed barriers, mismatched measures and teachers adapting programmes.
A principle is only useful if it rules something out, which is why 'support is temporary' counts and 'pupils should be supported to write well' does not.
The same sentence-combining practice failed as a standalone exercise and worked when built into pupils' own writing, showing the principle matters more than the practice.
Judging progress by supported work alone hides what pupils can do independently, so teachers should regularly look at writing produced once the help is gone.
quotes: A practice looked promising. Then it was tested more widely, and the effect shrank, disappeared, or turned out to depend on something else.
A class of “struggling writers” includes pupils whose hands can’t keep up, pupils whose sentences run on, pupils who don’t know enough, and pupils protecting themselves from failure.
A practice is the thing you do. A principle is the reason it works when it does work. When results contradict each other, looking at the principle often explains why.
The practice was the same in both cases; whether it was used in the writing it was meant for was what differed.

A principle is only useful if it rules something out. “Pupils should be supported to write well” isn’t a principle, because nobody disagrees with it and it forbids nothing. “Support is temporary” is a principle.
The scaffolded piece in the book shows what pupils can do with help. Regularly look at what they write when the help is gone, and plan from that.
I don’t want to swap it for another label. A label is what got us here, because it tells us how a pupil looks and not what they need.
Research can’t tell us which of our pupils is which. Principles tell us how to find out, and what to do once we know.
